pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 7-9 (Lower KS2/Grades 2-4): three survival strategies — CAMOUFLAGE (stick/leaf insects hide by blending in), WARNING COLOURS (wasp stripes say 'I'm dangerous'), and MIMICRY (harmless hoverfly copies a wasp to fool predators). The 'can you spot it?' challenge.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 Y4 'Living things and their habitats' (adaptation to environment); Y6 'Evolution and inheritance' (adaptation, foreshadowed).
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS4-3 (in a particular habitat some organisms survive well, some less well); 3-LS3-2 / 4-LS1-1 (structures/behaviours for survival).
• Operational details — the unifying idea is FUNCTION: each strategy helps the insect avoid being eaten, but by different logic (hide vs advertise vs impersonate). Frame everything from the PREDATOR'S point of view — why does the trick work? Warning colours only work because bright = memorable-after-a-bad-experience; mimicry only works because a real danger exists to copy. Keep it as observed phenomenon here; natural-selection mechanism comes at 9-11.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7): gives an example of camouflage. Tier B (age 8): explains why wasp warning stripes help it survive. Tier C (age 9): explains mimicry (harmless copies dangerous to trick predators) and contrasts the three strategies by how each fools/deters a predator.
bestPractices: Frame every strategy from the PREDATOR'S point of view — the trick only matters because of how it affects the eater.
Keep the three strategies distinct by their logic: hide (camouflage), advertise danger (warning colours), impersonate danger (mimicry).
Treat it as observed phenomenon at this age; save the natural-selection mechanism for 9-11.
Use 'can you spot it?' challenges so children experience camouflage's effectiveness first-hand.
Show the mimic beside its model so the copying is obvious (hoverfly vs wasp).
keyRepresentations: A 'spot the hidden insect' habitat scene (stick/leaf insects).
A mimic-and-model pairing (hoverfly next to wasp).
A three-way sort by strategy (camouflage / warning / mimicry).
commonMisconceptions: 'Camouflage means the insect chooses/decides to hide' — it's a fixed appearance, not a deliberate act.
'Bright colours are just for looking pretty' — warning colours function to deter predators.
'A mimic is actually dangerous' — the whole point is it's harmless but LOOKS dangerous.
'Predators are stupid to be fooled' — the tricks exploit sensible predator learning/avoidance.
Confusing warning colours (real danger, advertised) with mimicry (fake danger, borrowed).

learn.summary: For ages 7-9: teach three insect anti-predator strategies — camouflage (hiding by blending in), warning colours (bright patterns advertising 'I'm dangerous'), and mimicry (a harmless insect copying a dangerous one). The unifying idea is FUNCTION: each strategy helps an insect avoid being eaten, but by different logic (hide vs. advertise vs. impersonate). Frame everything from the predator's point of view — why does each trick work on the eater? Treat it as observed phenomenon here; the natural-selection mechanism comes later (ages 9-11).

activities.title: Play the hungry bird: feeling why each trick works
feedback: If camouflaged prey is missed repeatedly, point out: 'You couldn't find it — that's exactly why it survives.'
After the yuck penalty, prompt: 'What did that bright pattern just teach you to do next time?'
At the hoverfly reveal: 'It can't sting at all — but you avoided it because it LOOKED like something that could. That's the whole trick of mimicry.'

If a child thinks a brightly coloured bug must be worse off because predators can easily see it, contrast the two functions: a stick insect’s appearance makes it harder to notice, while a wasp’s conspicuous warning pattern makes it easier for predators to recognise and avoid — both can reduce the chance of being eaten.
If a child treats the three as the same, contrast them: one hides, one advertises real danger, one copies danger it doesn't have.
activities.rationale: Survival value may be grasped by taking the predator's role and feeling the live consequence (eat/avoid, hunger score). An interactive eat/avoid game can make 'why the trick works' felt from the eater's side rather than merely stated. The eat-penalty-then-hesitate sequence is one way to make the learning mechanism concrete; it is an optional design, not the only route and not shown to be superior to other media.
sourceClaims: Camouflage (crypsis), aposematism (warning colouration), and Batesian mimicry (harmless species resembling harmful ones) are established anti-predator strategies.
In a particular habitat some [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-LS4-3] (3-LS4-3); structures and behaviours help organisms survive.
learnerActions: Take the role of a hungry bird hunting bugs across leafy, twiggy backgrounds; tap prey to 'eat' them.

Notice that camouflaged insects are genuinely hard to find — a 'twig' turns out to be a stick insect, a 'leaf' turns out to be a leaf insect — so the hidden ones survive because you (the predator) can't spot them.
Eat a bold black-and-yellow caterpillar and receive a 'yuck' penalty; next time that bright pattern appears, decide whether to leave it.
When a harmless hoverfly appears wearing wasp stripes, decide whether to eat or avoid it, then reveal that it was a harmless bluff.
Afterwards, state in your own words how camouflage, warning colours, and mimicry each led to 'not eaten'.
activities.intendedInsight: Experiencing all three tricks from the eater's side: camouflage hides, warning colours teach the predator a lesson, and mimicry borrows someone else's scary reputation — all so the insect does not get eaten.

activities.title: Spot it and reveal it: a 'can you spot it?' habitat scene
feedback: If the mimic and model are confused, place them side by side: 'Which one can actually sting? Look again — their patterns are nearly the same.'
If a child says the hidden insect 'wasn't there before', reinforce: 'It was there the whole time — it just blended in.'
On the brown-soil prediction: 'A green leaf insect stands out on bare brown soil — camouflage only hides you when you match what's around you.'
activities.rationale: A rich reveal scene with linked callouts teaches recognition and the three categories cleanly, and a background-mismatch prediction surfaces that camouflage is context-dependent. It is a strong scaffold for naming and sorting, though on its own it shows the categories rather than running the predator-choice consequence that lets a learner feel why each works.
sourceClaims: Camouflage (crypsis), aposematism (warning colouration), and Batesian mimicry (harmless species resembling harmful ones) are established anti-predator strategies.
learnerActions: Search a busy habitat picture to find hidden stick and leaf insects; tap or point to reveal each one.
For bright-coloured bugs, open a callout explaining what the colour is telling predators.
For a wasp-and-hoverfly pairing, identify which look-alike is the harmless mimic and which is the real danger.
Count how many camouflaged insects you missed on the first pass to feel how well hiding works.

Predict what would happen to a green leaf insect placed on bare brown soil instead of green leaves — would it still be hidden? — and explain why matching the background matters for camouflage to work.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising the three categories first-hand: camouflaged insects are hard to find, warning colours are a message, and a mimic can look very similar to its model — and seeing that camouflage only works when the insect's appearance matches its surroundings, so it can fail on the wrong background.

activities.title: Sort and explain the strategies
feedback: If warning colours are called 'just pretty', re-frame: bright is a message — 'stay away, I might sting or taste bad' — not decoration.
If the hoverfly is said to 'really sting because it has stripes', clarify: it cannot sting; looking dangerous is enough to borrow the protection.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and short-answer explanation assess the distinctions and the function of warning colours. Sorting and matching can check recognition; asking for a justification pushes toward explaining function. A sort by itself checks classification but does not on its own elicit the learner's independent construction of the reasoning, so the justification step is what probes explanation.
sourceClaims: Camouflage (crypsis), aposematism (warning colouration), and Batesian mimicry (harmless species resembling harmful ones) are established anti-predator strategies.
learnerActions: Sort a set of insects into three groups: camouflage, warning colours, and mimicry.
Match each mimic to the dangerous model it copies (hoverfly to wasp).
Answer: 'Why do a wasp's bright stripes help it survive?' and justify your choice.
Explain in a sentence why a harmless hoverfly with wasp stripes is still left alone by predators.
activities.intendedInsight: The three strategies are distinguished by their logic, and warning colours work because a predator often learns to avoid that pattern after a bad experience with it.

activities.title: Ask the bird (optional dialogue)
feedback: If the learner thinks predators are 'stupid' to be fooled, reframe: the tricks exploit sensible learning — avoiding things that hurt you is smart.
activities.rationale: A light dialogue can surface the predator's-eye logic in words and may suit learners who explain best by talking. It is offered as an alternative with a different purpose (verbalising reasoning), not a replacement for the experiential game and not claimed to be more or less effective.
learnerActions: Interview a bird character: 'Why don't you eat the stripy ones?' and 'Why did you leave the hoverfly alone?'
Press further: 'What happened the first time you tried to eat something stripy?' to surface the learned-avoidance logic.
Use the bird's answers to write or say why each strategy keeps an insect from being eaten.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the predator's reasoning into words — avoidance often follows a bad experience, and a convincing copy earns the same avoidance.

constraints: Treat these as observed phenomena at this age; do not introduce the natural-selection mechanism, which belongs at ages 9-11.

The inherited colour and pattern adaptations discussed here were not deliberately designed or chosen by the insect. This does not mean insects cannot choose hiding places or display behaviour; avoid suggesting that an individual hoverfly decided to evolve wasp-like stripes.
Camouflage is context-dependent: it conceals only when the insect's appearance matches its background, so it can fail in the wrong setting (e.g. a green leaf insect on bare brown soil).

A reveal/spotting scene teaches recognition and categories; it shows rather than lets the learner feel the eat/avoid consequence, so pair it with an interactive or discussion activity if the goal is 'why it works'. This is an affordance of that format, not proof any medium is superior.

Sorting and multiple-choice can confirm recognition and can check reasoning when a justification is required, but recognition-only responses do not by themselves elicit the learner's independent construction of the explanation.

Keep the three strategies distinct by logic: hide (camouflage), advertise real danger (warning colours), impersonate danger the insect does not have (mimicry). Do not blur warning colours (real, advertised danger) with mimicry (fake, borrowed danger).
The eat-penalty / hesitation sequence and side-by-side mimic-model pairing are optional illustrative designs, not required mechanisms or validated interventions.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source claims in this row are marked verified:false in the original; treat them as unconfirmed. Do not assume empirical testing of any activity here.

The original framed the predator-role 2D game as 'best' and implied other formats 'can't' show why each strategy works; this comparative/necessity claim is not established by the sources and has been softened to scoped proposals.
The context counterexample — a leaf insect on bare brown soil — is included in the spotting activity: camouflage depends on matching the background, so it can fail in the wrong setting.
The 'only hiding can protect' misconception is now explicitly addressed in the hungry-bird feedback by contrasting avoiding notice (stick insect) with wanting to be noticed-then-avoided (wasp).
The hoverfly second tier (looking dangerous vs. being dangerous) is noted in the source as the key discriminator for whether a learner grasps that the signal, not the sting, does the protecting.
Aposematism avoidance is treated here as learned after a bad experience, an age-appropriate simplification; the full mechanism (including possible innate avoidance) is not asserted.

probeDeeper: 'Why does the wasp WANT to be seen, but the stick insect wants NOT to be seen — aren't they opposites? How can both keep the insect alive?'
'The hoverfly can't sting at all. So why do predators still leave it alone?'
'A leaf insect on bare brown soil instead of green leaves — would its camouflage still work? Why not?' (context counterexample)
'What does a bird have to experience ONCE for the wasp's warning to work on it afterwards?'
assess.correctAnswer: The stick insect uses camouflage — blending in so predators can't spot it to eat it. The wasp's bright stripes are a warning: they tell predators 'I can sting — leave me alone', so predators learn to avoid it. The harmless hoverfly uses mimicry — it copies the wasp's warning colours, so predators avoid it too even though it can't actually sting; it gets the protection without the sting.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks bright warning colours are for decoration or to attract mates/friends, not to warn predators away
errorPatterns.nextMove: Frame colour as a message to predators: 'stay away, I'll hurt you'. Ask what a bird learns after being stung once — it avoids the pattern next time. Bright can mean danger, not beauty.
errorPatterns.distractor: The wasp's bright stripes are just to look pretty / to attract other wasps
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the wasp is 'showing off' or 'being pretty'; can't say bright = danger signal

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks only hiding can protect an animal — can't see how being EASY to spot could ever help
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the two jobs: the stick insect avoids being noticed; the wasp WANTS to be noticed so it's avoided. Both end with 'not eaten' by different routes.
errorPatterns.distractor: Being bright and easy to see is always bad — it helps predators find it
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists the wasp's bright colours must be bad for it because predators can see it; treats standing out as always dangerous

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the harmless hoverfly copies the wasp on purpose / chose to, or that it must actually be able to sting
errorPatterns.nextMove: Clarify the trick: the hoverfly can't sting at all, but LOOKS dangerous, so predators avoid it just in case. It didn't choose its colours — they help it survive (adaptation is set up in the next topic). Distinguish looking dangerous from being dangerous.
errorPatterns.distractor: The hoverfly must really be able to sting, because it has the stripes
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: says the hoverfly decided to look like a wasp, or insists it must really sting because it has the stripes

responseLevels.gap: Thinks bright colours are decorative, or that only hiding can protect; can't explain the hoverfly at all.
responseLevels.full: Explains camouflage AND warning colours as two routes to 'not eaten', AND explains mimicry — the harmless hoverfly borrows the wasp's warning signal so predators avoid it — transferring the idea (e.g. sees camouflage fails on the wrong background), showing the signal does the work.
responseLevels.partial: Explains camouflage (hiding) and can say bright colours warn, but treats them as unrelated facts — can't explain mimicry, i.e. why a harmless insect copying a dangerous one gets protection.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A wasp has bright yellow-and-black stripes that are easy to spot, but a stick insect is hard to see because it looks just like a twig. Both of these help the insect stay alive — how? And a harmless hoverfly ALSO has yellow-and-black stripes even though it has no sting. Why would that help it?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands survival signalling can hold BOTH strategies at once — hiding (camouflage) AND standing out (warning) both protect — and can explain mimicry as borrowing a warning. A child with a shallow 'bright = pretty, bright = attracts friends' idea says the wasp's colours are to look nice or attract mates, and can't explain why a harmless fly would copy a dangerous one. The hoverfly second tier is the discriminator: it only makes sense if you grasp that the SIGNAL, not the sting, does the protecting.
